readerTitle: The growth plan that looks slower in year one
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 서비스, IT 지원 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 성장이나 손실이 '고정된 양'인지 '이미 가진 것의 일정 비율'인지 먼저 구분한다. 비율로 쌓이는 쪽은 처음엔 느려 보여도 시간이 갈수록 격차가 커진다.
misconception: 매달 꾸준히 같은 수를 더하는 계획이 더 안전하고 결국 비슷한 결과를 낸다. 1~3% 같은 작은 비율 차이는 신경 쓸 만큼 크지 않다.

sources.text: 복리 계산과 72의 법칙: 표준 수학 근사식

factChecks.note: 72의 법칙: 72 ÷ 3 = 24개월. 실제 두 배가 되는 기간은 ln2 ÷ ln1.03 ≈ 23.4개월입니다. 감소 쪽 근사(72 ÷ 2 = 36개월, 실제 0.98^n = 0.5에서 n ≈ 34.3개월)는 카드에 'roughly'로 적었습니다.
손실 복리: 0.98^12 = 0.785(약 78% 유지), 0.97^12 = 0.694(약 69% 유지). 이 계산은 신규 유입 없이 한 묶음의 고객이 얼마나 남는지를 보는 기준입니다.
첫 판단 문제는 단순화를 위해 고객 이탈이 없다고 가정했습니다. 카드 2 본문에 이 가정을 밝혔습니다.

cards.title: Two ways to grow a cleaning business
body: Maya runs a home cleaning service with 100 regular clients. She is choosing between two ways to grow.
**Plan A:** flyers that bring in 3 new clients every month, like clockwork. **Plan B:** a referral reward where every 100 clients bring in about 3 new ones a month.
In the first month, both plans add exactly 3 clients.

image.label: A cleaner choosing between two paths: a stack of flyers and a chain of houses
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 청소 도구를 든 사업가가 갈림길에 서 있음. 왼쪽 길에는 전단지 더미, 오른쪽 길에는 집들이 점선으로 연결되어 한 집이 다른 집을 소개하는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: After three years, which plan has more clients?
body: To keep it simple, assume no client ever leaves. Both plans cost about the same to run.

options.text: Plan A. Steady and predictable wins
options.feedback: A fixed number is easier to plan around, but 3 a month stays 3 forever. Plan B's monthly gain grows with every client it adds.

options.text: About the same. They start out identical
options.feedback: True for the first year: 136 versus 143. After that, the gap widens every single month.

options.text: Plan B, by a wide margin
options.feedback: Right. About 290 clients versus 208. In Plan B, new clients go on to bring in clients of their own.

cards.title: Same start, very different endings.
body: After one year, the plans are only 7 clients apart. After three years, Plan B leads by 82, and most of that gap opened in the final year.

cards.title: Compounding
body: **Compounding** happens when each period's gain joins the base, and the next gain is figured on that bigger base. The growth starts to produce more growth.
The quick test: is the gain a fixed amount, or a share of what you already have? Fixed amounts add up in a straight line. Shares of a growing base bend upward.

image.label: A straight line and an upward curve that start at the same point
image.brief: 단순한 그래프 인포그래픽. 같은 점에서 출발한 직선("+3 a month")과 위로 휘는 곡선("+3% a month"). 초반에는 거의 겹치고 오른쪽 끝에서 크게 벌어짐. 벌어진 구간을 은은하게 강조.

cards.title: Most of the payoff arrives late.
body: Compounding feels slow at first because the base is small. The big gains only show up once the base has grown.

A handy check is the **rule of 72**: divide 72 by the growth rate per period to estimate how many periods it takes to double. At 3% a month, Maya's list doubles in about 24 months, then starts doubling again from 200.
This is why people often drop compounding plans too early. In year one, they look no better than the steady option.

cards.title: Small losses compound too.
body: The same math works in reverse. A business that loses 2% of its clients each month keeps only about 78% of them after a year, and the leak keeps eating into whatever is left.
Anything that shrinks by a share each period behaves this way: clients, repeat orders, a team's know-how. A small, steady leak deserves the same attention as a small, steady gain.
cards.softwareNote: Monthly churn, the share of paying users who cancel each month, compounds. At 3% a month, you keep only about 69% of a group of users after a year, which is why cutting churn often beats a one-off launch spike.

cards.title: Rates rarely hold forever.
body: Compounding assumes the rate stays the same. Real rates tend to fall. Maya's town has only so many homes, and her clients' friends start to overlap.
Capacity limits it too. She can't clean 290 homes without hiring and training people, and quality may slip while she does.
A curve drawn from a few good months can promise far more than the market or the team can deliver. Use compounding to compare options, not to forecast exact numbers.

image.label: An upward curve flattening as it hits a ceiling
image.brief: 위로 휘던 곡선이 점선으로 된 천장("Market size", "Team capacity")에 가까워지며 완만해지는 그래프. 차분한 색조, 경고 느낌의 작은 아이콘 하나.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: You provide IT support to 40 small offices. Your team is buried in repeat tickets: printer failures, password resets, the same email problem every week.
You can free up some time to deal with it. Which approach pays off most over a year?

options.text: Hire a temp for a month to clear the backlog
options.feedback: The queue shrinks fast, but nothing changes underneath. A month later the same tickets are back.

options.text: Spend one intense week on a full system cleanup, then return to normal
options.feedback: You get a real drop in tickets. But it's a single step down, not a gain that keeps building.

options.text: Each week, permanently fix the most common cause of repeat tickets
options.feedback: Each fix shrinks future work and frees time for the next fix, so the gains stack. Expect later fixes to be harder than the first few.

cards.title: Ask whether a gain grows itself.
body: Fixed gains add up. Gains that are a share of a growing base compound, and so do small losses. Judge those plans over years, not months.

**Try it today:** pick one thing in your business that grows or shrinks by a share each month, like referrals or repeat orders. Estimate the rate, then divide 72 by it to see roughly how long until it doubles or halves.
